st.t: Cross-border outsourcing: Oversight follows the provider chain
st.an: The Commission accepts that outsourcing leaves lawyers’ existing professional duties intact and materially develops the cluster’s context-sensitive approach by proposing targeted Model Rule Comments for outside lawyers, nonlawyers and unauthorized-practice risks rather than new rule text or bright-line standards.
qs: The ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20 has concluded that, although changes to the text of the Model Rules are not necessary, Comments to certain Rules should be clarified to address this issue so that lawyers can more easily determine their ethical obligations.
Finally, the Commission proposes a new sentence to Comment [1] to Model Rule 5.5 to clarify that lawyers cannot engage in outsourcing when doing so would facilitate the unauthorized practice of law.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, human-accountable deployment and materially extends the cluster with a principles-based ethics framework for outsourced and automated nonlawyer assistance. It makes competence, provider selection, confidentiality, context-sensitive oversight and allocation of monitoring responsibility central, while rejecting rigid rules for diverse and evolving arrangements.

st.t: AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s distinction between continuing supervisory responsibility and automatic liability. It applies existing competence and Rule 5.3 duties to external and automated services, requires context-sensitive safeguards and instructions, and limits responsibility for misconduct to ordering, knowing ratification, or a knowing failure to take reasonable remedial action.

st.t: Outsourcing fees: Delegation cannot justify double recovery
st.an: The Commission supports applying existing professional duties to outsourcing rather than creating a separate regime. It reinforces competence, confidentiality, monitoring and unauthorized-practice obligations, while treating existing fee rules and ethics guidance as sufficient; it therefore aligns with the cluster’s rejection of outsourcing as a basis for duplicative charges, though it does not itself develop the cluster’s detailed distinction between service fees, pass-through costs and double recovery.
qs: The ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20 has concluded that, although changes to the text of the Model Rules are not necessary, Comments to certain Rules should be clarified to address this issue so that lawyers can more easily determine their ethical obligations.

The Commission reached the same conclusion about Model Rule 1.5 (Fees) and the wealth of ethics opinions available treating myriad specific questions relating to the reasonableness of fees for both legal and non-legal services, as well as regarding Model Rule 1.15 (Safekeeping Property).

st.t: Technology competence: Delegation preserves professional responsibility
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: outsourcing does not displace lawyers’ duties of competence, confidentiality and ethical representation. It requires context-sensitive selection, client consent, appropriate direction and monitoring, while preserving the lawyer’s professional responsibility.

kp.k: Existing ethical principles govern evolving outsourcing arrangements
kp.d: The Commission proposes clarifying the Comments to Model Rules 1.1, 5.3 and 5.5, and changing Rule 5.3’s title, rather than changing substantive rule text. This 2012 report addresses outsourcing and automated assistance, including cloud computing, rather than AI specifically. It presents context-sensitive guidance that supplements, rather than replaces, malpractice, tort and other applicable law. The filing requests adoption; it does not establish subsequent adoption or state implementation.
qs: In each of these cases, the Commission’s goal is to clarify how existing rules and principles apply to the particular context of outsourcing.
The Commission’s proposals also reflect the view that the evolution of law practice and the continued rapid changes in and diversity of outsourcing arrangements make bright lines impossible to draw.

kp.k: Technology and client demand enable disaggregated legal work
kp.d: The Commission attributes outsourcing growth to globalization, providers’ technology-driven efficiencies and client demand for cost-effective services. Tasks include research, document review, patent searches, due diligence, contract drafting, discovery databases and online storage. Its research indicates domestic outsourcing remained more common than international outsourcing, with providers responding to demand for additional onshore operations; no quantitative market estimates are supplied.
qs: Among the factors that have contributed to the significant growth of outsourcing are globalization, the technology-driven efficiencies developed and utilized by many providers of outsourced services, and the demand by clients for cost-effective services.
The Commission’s research indicates that lawyers still tend to outsource legal and law-related work domestically more often than they outsource work internationally.

kp.k: Outsourcing offers conditional efficiency and access benefits
kp.d: The report states that careful provider selection can enable faster, cheaper work without sacrificing quality, helping solo and smaller firms resource large matters. It presents improved access to justice through affordability as a possibility, not a measured outcome. Acknowledging lawyers’ employment hardships, the Commission expressly neither endorses nor rejects outsourcing.
qs: In particular, lawyers have found that, if they exercise proper care in the selection of a provider, work can be completed with greater speed and lower costs without sacrificing quality.
Also, by reducing the cost of legal services, outsourcing can improve access to justice by making legal services more affordable.
The changes to the Comments to Rules 1.1, 5.3, and 5.5 of the Model Rules of Professional Conduct are neither an endorsement nor a rejection of the practice of outsourcing.

kp.k: Provider safeguards inform the Commission’s qualitative findings
kp.d: Drawing on studies, surveys, scholarship, hearings, submissions, news and provider materials, the Commission reports provider investment in confidentiality safeguards, security, conflicts checking and training. Examples include confidentiality agreements, encryption, physical access controls, audits and conflicts databases. These are reported practices among many or some providers, not universal compliance findings or quantified demonstrations of effectiveness.
qs: The Commission also reviewed materials from domestic and international outsourcing providers, finding substantial evidence that the providers are focused on the ethical considerations identified in the organized bars’ ethics opinions.
For example, a number of outsourcing providers employ conflicts checking procedures modeled after those used by large U.S. and U.K. law firms; others are developing similar systems.

The Commission’s research has revealed that a number of companies that provide outsourced services have established sophisticated training programs for nonlawyer and lawyer employees on a variety of topics, including U.S. substantive and procedural law, legal research and writing, and the rules of professional conduct.

kp.k: Nonfirm lawyer retention requires competence and ordinarily consent
kp.d: Proposed Rule 1.1 commentary emphasizes competent and ethical representation, ordinarily obtaining informed client consent, and assessing outside lawyers’ education, experience, reputation, assigned services and jurisdictional protections, particularly confidentiality. Consent is not described as invariably necessary: a discrete, limited task without confidential disclosure may be an exception. Multiple firms should ordinarily consult with each other and the client about scope and responsibility.
qs: The first sentence also explains that, ordinarily, a lawyer should obtain a client’s informed consent before retaining a nonfirm lawyer.

The Commission was reluctant to conclude that consent is always required, because consent may not be necessary when a nonfirm lawyer is hired to perform a discrete and limited task, especially if the task does not require the disclosure of confidential information.
This list is not intended to be exhaustive, but is intended to give lawyers some guidance regarding some of the most important considerations to take into account when retaining nonfirm lawyers.

kp.k: Outside-lawyer oversight requirements remain deliberately unresolved
kp.d: The Commission removed draft language requiring a reasonable belief that the outside lawyer’s work had been competently performed after accepting concerns about unnecessary, costly competency-checking obligations. Because arrangements vary, it requested more nuanced treatment of oversight in an ethics opinion rather than prescribing its extent in a Model Rule Comment.
qs: In early drafts of this proposal, the Commission had an additional sentence at the end of the Comment that would have required lawyers to reasonably believe that the nonfirm lawyer’s work was competently performed.
The Commission concluded that these concerns were well-founded.

Because the outsourcing of work to other lawyers takes many different forms, the Commission concluded that the level of oversight over those lawyers should be addressed in an ethics opinion, which can provide a nuanced treatment of the issue, rather than in a Comment to the Model Rules.

kp.k: Nonlawyer assistance includes automated services outside firms
kp.d: The proposed Rule 5.3 title change from “Nonlawyer Assistants” to “Nonlawyer Assistance” reflects coverage of automated products as well as people. The commentary calls for reasonable efforts and appropriate instructions to align external services with lawyers’ professional obligations. Relevant circumstances include provider qualifications, service type, information-protection arrangements and the jurisdiction’s legal and ethical environment.
qs: As an initial matter, proposed Comment [3] recognizes that nonlawyer services can take many forms, including services performed by individuals and services performed by automated products (e.g., online data storage).
The last sentence of Comment [3] emphasizes that lawyers have an obligation to give appropriate instructions to nonlawyers outside the firm when retaining or directing those nonlawyers.

kp.k: Nonlawyer disclosure consent depends on the circumstances
kp.d: The Commission intentionally leaves consent requirements for disclosures to external nonlawyer providers unspecified in the proposed commentary. Routine scanning or copying ordinarily does not require consent, while other arrangements may make consent advisable or required. It requests further ethics-committee clarification rather than imposing a blanket rule.
qs: Notably, the proposed Comment language does not describe whether a lawyer must obtain consent when disclosing confidential information to nonlawyer service providers outside the firm.
For example, lawyers regularly send documents to outside vendors for scanning or copying, but there is ordinarily no need to obtain the client’s consent to have those services performed.
There are, however, other situations where client consent might be advisable or required.

kp.k: Client-selected providers require explicit monitoring allocations
kp.d: The Commission distinguishes monitoring from direct supervision when an external provider cannot readily be supervised. Where clients select providers, lawyers and clients should ordinarily allocate monitoring responsibility; otherwise it rests with the lawyer or firm. Tribunal obligations may prevent complete transfer to the client, particularly where a lawyer must make representations concerning an electronic discovery vendor’s work.
qs: The word “monitoring” reflects a new ethical concept.

The Commission concluded that it was needed because, when a nonlawyer outside the firm is performing services in connection with a matter, it may not be possible to “directly supervise” the nonlawyer.
In contrast, if the client has not directed the selection of the nonlawyer, the lawyer or law firm would have the “monitoring” responsibility.

For example, if a client instructs the lawyer to hire a particular electronic discovery vendor, the lawyer cannot cede all monitoring responsibility to the client, given that the lawyer may have to make certain representations to a tribunal regarding the vendor’s work.

kp.k: Outsourcing cannot facilitate unauthorized legal practice
kp.d: The proposed addition to Rule 5.5 commentary makes explicit that outsourcing to lawyers or nonlawyers must not facilitate unauthorized practice. This clarifies an existing professional restriction rather than creating permission for external providers to practise law.
qs: When lawyers outsource work to lawyers and nonlawyers, it is important to ensure that those lawyers and nonlawyers are not engaging in the unauthorized practice of law.
The Commission concluded that it is important to make this point explicitly in Comment [1] to Model Rule 5.5.

kp.k: Evolving outsourcing calls for continuing guidance and education
kp.d: The Commission recommends continued study and professional education as arrangements evolve and new ethical issues arise. It favors an updateable ABA resource over a static set of practice standards, which it considers premature during rapid change.
qs: The Commission believes that continued study by, and education of, the profession about outsourcing practices is essential, especially given that those practices will evolve and new ethics issues may arise.
This website will provide up-to-date access to both evolving outsourcing practices and the technological changes that make them possible.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Commission makes no AI-specific claims. Its related claims concern technology-enabled outsourcing, automated nonlawyer assistance, and their effects on legal delivery and professional obligations.
pts.d: In this 2012 filing, the ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20 attributes increasing disaggregation and outsourcing of legal work to technology, globalization, and client demand for cost-effective services. It states that appropriately selected outsourcing providers can deliver work faster and at lower cost without sacrificing quality; that this can help smaller firms compete for large matters; and that lower costs can improve access to justice. It also reports that domestic outsourcing remains more common than international outsourcing and that providers are responding to demand for onshore operations. These are claims about outsourcing, not findings about AI. The Commission explicitly includes automated products such as online storage within nonlawyer assistance and proposes clarifying existing ethical obligations rather than creating a separate regulatory regime. It anticipates evolving practices and possible new ethical issues, without forecasting AI capabilities or lawyer replacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The stated basis is qualitative research, professional experience, consultation, provider materials, and ethics authority; the filing supplies no quantified outcome estimates or AI evaluations.
pts.d: The Commission identifies scholarly articles, studies, surveys, public testimony, stakeholder comments, news reports, and provider materials as informing its conclusions. It attributes the speed, cost, and quality claim broadly to what lawyers have found, without identifying a particular comparative study or supplying measurements. Smaller-firm competitiveness and access-to-justice benefits are presented as opportunities rather than measured outcomes. Its research reports provider confidentiality agreements, security controls, audits, conflicts systems, and training programs as evidence of attention to ethical requirements, not proof that every provider achieves equivalent quality or security. The ethical proposals draw particularly on ABA Formal Opinion 08-451 and other bar opinions. No AI benchmarks, hallucination measurements, or AI deployment cases appear.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims describe trends observed by 2012 and open-ended future evolution; efficiency benefits depend on provider selection, and outsourcing remains subject to context-sensitive professional obligations.
pts.d: The report was submitted for the August 2012 Annual Meeting and presents the amendments as proposals, not evidence of adoption by individual jurisdictions. It gives no numerical forecast or deadline for future market change. The claim of faster, cheaper work without quality loss expressly depends on proper care in selecting providers. Proposed guidance makes obligations depend on the provider, assigned services, confidentiality arrangements, and relevant jurisdictions. Informed consent ordinarily applies to retaining outside lawyers, but the report allows limited exceptions; consent for outside nonlawyer services is also context-dependent. Monitoring responsibilities may be allocated with clients who select providers, but tribunal obligations can prevent a lawyer from relinquishing all oversight. The Commission neither endorses nor rejects outsourcing and regards rapidly evolving arrangements as unsuitable for rigid standards.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source identifies opportunities for smaller firms and clients, continuing responsibilities for lawyers and corporate counsel, operational demands on outside providers, and employment concerns for job-seeking lawyers.
pts.d: Solo practitioners and small and medium-sized US firms are said to gain access to resources that let them compete for larger matters. Clients may obtain lower-cost services, while improved affordability is presented separately as a potential access-to-justice benefit. Law firms, individual lawyers, and corporate counsel increasingly outsource tasks including research, document review, due diligence, drafting, discovery support, and data storage. Lawyers remain responsible for reasonable provider selection, instructions, monitoring, confidentiality protection, and avoiding assistance in unauthorized practice. Clients who select nonlawyer providers may share monitoring responsibilities. Outside lawyers, nonlawyer service providers, and automated-service vendors are covered by different aspects of the proposed guidance; they should not all be treated as AI vendors or ALSPs. The report acknowledges controversy amid employment hardship but does not quantify job displacement or claim that technology caused it.
